question: What is the main drawback of vertical scaling (Scale Up)?

options.text: Complex setup — requires changing the application architecture
options.explanation: The opposite: Scale Up doesn't require code or architecture changes. You simply increase server resources

options.text: Hardware power limits and exponential cost growth
options.explanation: The maximum server has a physical ceiling (e.g., 448 vCPU on AWS). And each doubling of power costs disproportionately more — the cost curve is superlinear

options.text: Requires a load balancer
options.explanation: A load balancer is needed for horizontal scaling (Scale Out) with multiple servers. With Scale Up, there's only one server

options.text: Databases cannot be scaled vertically
options.explanation: Databases are often scaled vertically — adding RAM for cache, fast SSDs for I/O. This is a common practice, especially at early stages

question: What makes a service stateless and why is this important for horizontal scaling?

options.text: A stateless service doesn't use a database
options.explanation: Stateless means the server doesn't store client state in its own memory. It can still access an external DB — that's actually recommended for storing state

options.text: A stateless service doesn't store client state in server memory — any instance can handle any request
options.explanation: When a server doesn't store sessions/state in its memory, a request can be routed to any of N servers. This makes horizontal scaling simple — just add servers behind a load balancer

options.text: A stateless service doesn't handle POST requests, only GET
options.explanation: Stateless is unrelated to HTTP methods. A service can handle any requests, the key is not storing client state in process memory between requests

options.text: A stateless service restarts after every request
options.explanation: A stateless service runs continuously, like any other. It just doesn't save client data in RAM between requests

question: What axes are included in the Scaling Cube (AKF Scale Cube)?

options.text: X-axis — cloning: running identical copies of the service behind a load balancer
options.explanation: X-axis (Horizontal Duplication) — the simplest scaling method: N identical application instances handle requests in parallel

options.text: Y-axis — functional decomposition: splitting into microservices by business function
options.explanation: Y-axis (Functional Decomposition) — a monolith is split into separate services (Auth, Catalog, Orders), each scaling independently

options.text: Z-axis — data partitioning: splitting data across servers by key (sharding)
options.explanation: Z-axis (Data Partitioning) — data is split by key (e.g., User ID) across multiple servers/DBs, each handling its own range

options.text: W-axis — geographic distribution: placing servers in different regions
options.explanation: The AKF Scale Cube model has only three axes: X, Y, and Z. Geographic distribution is a separate concept (multi-region deployment), not part of the Scaling Cube

question: You have an e-commerce application with 5% sequential code (writes to leader DB). By Amdahl's Law, what is the maximum speedup you can achieve with an infinite number of servers?

options.explanation: Maximum speedup = 1/S, where S is the sequential fraction. 1/0.05 = 20x. Even infinite servers cannot exceed this limit
By Amdahl's Law: Speedup(max) = 1/S = 1/0.05 = 20x. This is the theoretical ceiling: 5% of code runs sequentially and cannot be parallelized, limiting overall speedup

options.text: Infinite — just keep adding servers
options.explanation: Amdahl's Law shows that a sequential code section (even 5%) creates a hard ceiling. Speedup(max) = 1/0.05 = 20x, no more
Speedup(max) = 1/S = 1/0.05 = 20x, not 50x. Even 2% sequential code would limit speedup to 1/0.02 = 50x

question: You use sticky sessions (session affinity) to scale a stateful service. In which scenario does this create a problem?

options.text: All users send the same number of requests
options.explanation: With uniform load, sticky sessions work acceptably. Problems begin with uneven distribution or failures

options.text: One server goes down — all users bound to it lose their sessions
options.explanation: Sticky sessions bind a client to a specific server. If that server fails, all its users lose state. Also, 'hot' clients overload one server while others idle

options.text: All servers have the same configuration
options.explanation: Identical configuration is normal and even desirable. Sticky session problems lie elsewhere: server failure = session loss, uneven load

options.text: Servers are located in the same data center
options.explanation: Location in the same data center doesn't affect sticky session problems. The issue is binding users to a specific server and the consequences of its failure
